claims.text: The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The as-built alloy contains fine dendritic structure and non-equilibrium phases characteristic of additive manufacturing.
Elevated-temperature degradation and catastrophic failure are primarily governed by the evolution of a transient, non-protective oxide scale.
An oxidizing atmosphere causes rapid growth of a porous, brittle oxide layer.
Oxide growth locally depletes key alloying elements near the oxide/alloy interface.
Oxide growth and associated elemental depletion embrittle grain boundaries.
The non-protective scale is likely to contain TiO2 and other mixed oxides.
Reducing atmospheres produce less oxide growth than oxidizing atmospheres.
Under reducing conditions, altered chemical potential at high temperature drives phase transformations or coarsening.
Phase transformations or coarsening under reducing conditions degrade mechanical integrity and intergranular cohesion.
Loss of intergranular cohesion can precipitate catastrophic failure in both oxidizing and reducing atmospheres.
High-temperature in situ diffraction or microscopy can monitor oxide formation and phase evolution in real time.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a rapidly thickening porous scale, interfacial elemental depletion, and early microcracks relative to the as-built state.
Reducing exposure will produce slower oxide growth but observable grain coarsening or precipitate evolution.
The reducing-atmosphere microstructural changes will correlate with reduced ductility and strength.
The as-built baseline has minimal oxide, an intact homogeneous FCC matrix, and a stable microstructure under ambient conditions.
The proposed governing behavior applies between approximately 700 and 1000 °C in controlled oxidizing and hydrogen/argon reducing atmospheres.
Observable oxide or phase-evolution indicators will precede catastrophic mechanical failure.
